nameStory: This microscopic green alga gets its species name 'tohopekaligense' from Lake Tohopekaliga in Florida, where it was first discovered and described by scientists. The genus name Staurastrum comes from Greek words meaning 'cross' and 'star,' referring to the beautiful star-like or cross-shaped appearance these tiny organisms display under a microscope.
description: Staurastrum tohopekaligense is a single-celled green alga that lives in freshwater environments, invisible to the naked eye but spectacular under magnification. Like other members of its genus, it has a symmetrical, star-like shape with radiating arms or processes extending from a central body. These microscopic organisms are typically only about 20-50 micrometers across (smaller than the width of a human hair) and contribute to the planktonic community in ponds and lakes. Each cell is bright green due to chlorophyll and helps form the base of aquatic food webs.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Completely invisible to naked eye - you'll need at least 400x magnification to see its intricate star-like structure clearly

idTips.label: Star-shaped symmetry
idTips.description: Displays perfect radial symmetry with arms or processes extending from central body like points of a star

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Rich emerald green coloration from chlorophyll, clearly visible under microscope lighting

idTips.label: Two-part cell structure
idTips.description: Cell appears pinched in the middle with two symmetrical halves (semicells) joined together

idTips.label: Planktonic lifestyle
idTips.description: Floats freely in water column rather than attached to surfaces - collect from open water

habitat: Found in freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, typically in slightly acidic to neutral waters. Prefers clean, nutrient-poor to moderately nutrient-rich environments and is often found floating in the open water column rather than near shores. Most commonly discovered in kettle ponds, mountain lakes, and pristine woodland pools.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures rise and daylight increases. Best time to find them as spring algal blooms develop in lakes and ponds.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance during warm months when conditions are optimal for photosynthesis and reproduction. Water samples from sunny, warm days often yield the best specimens.
seasonality.fall: Numbers typically decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases. Still present but may require more patient searching through water samples.
seasonality.winter: Populations at lowest levels under ice cover, but hardy individuals can survive in deeper waters. Rarely collected during this season.

funFact: Despite being smaller than a speck of dust, each Staurastrum cell is an architectural masterpiece that reproduces by literally splitting in half - each half then grows back the missing pieces to create two perfect copies, like biological 3D printing at the microscopic level!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other star-shaped Staurastrum species, but the specific arrangement and proportions of its radiating processes are unique. Remember that definitive identification usually requires detailed microscopic measurements and comparison with scientific illustrations, as many species in this genus look remarkably similar at first glance.
contextualKnowledge: This species is extremely rare in New England with only one documented observation, making it a significant find for any freshwater microscopist. Most people are amazed to learn that such intricate, beautiful organisms exist in ordinary pond water, representing an entire microscopic world of geometric perfection that's completely hidden from our daily experience.
compareHints: Distinguished from other New England Staurastrum species by its specific pattern of radiating arms and overall cell proportions, though definitive identification requires careful microscopic examination. Unlike the more common Staurastrum species with simpler projections, S. tohopekaligense has a distinctive arrangement that reflects its southern origins. Its rarity in New England also sets it apart from more frequently encountered relatives in the same genus.
